new_statements.rule_in_words: Yukuben is a three-tone language (H, M, L per Anyanwu's tonology) with no noticeable word stress; the only prominence asymmetry is phonetic: second/stem syllables whose vowel is reduced to schwa sound weaker than syllables with full vowels (Rennison's abstract adds that canonical disyllabic nouns show lengthening of the first syllable and schwa reduction in the second).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only qualification is the perceptual weakness of schwa syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic nouns = noun-class prefix + stem), based on the Vienna Yukuben corpus; the statement is made in a comparative theoretical paper, not in a dedicated grammar. Anyanwu's 2013 grammar (the fullest description, with a phonology part pp. 49-88 and a tonology part pp. 89-98) has no stress section in its table of contents and could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Rennison 2014 draws on the Vienna Yukuben corpus (project 2004-2007, Nigerian Yukuben); dialect not specified in the snippet. Anyanwu 2013 covers the two major dialects Bā-lāābɘn and Bá-líssà (also called Lissa and Nyairəm in Anyanwu 2009). Cameroonian Yukuben (Uhumghikgi; ELAR elicitations by Jeff Good's team) is the same glottocode yuku1243; the newly reported sister language Baazəm is baaz1234, not covered here.

new_statements.quote: Eine weitere Unterscheidung der Vokale im Yukuben gibt es durch die drei Töne: hoch (´), mittel (¯), tief (`). Es gibt keinen Druckakzent.
new_statements.translation: A further distinction among the vowels in Yukuben is made by the three tones: high (´), mid (¯), low (`). There is no stress accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement from Rennison 2014 ('Yukuben and Mòoré have no noticeable word stress..') and with the catalog's tone-language reading: three lexical tones, no stress. Weitzenauer is categorical ('keinen Druckakzent') where Rennison hedges ('no noticeable word stress, although syllables with schwa.. sound weaker'); the two are compatible. Source obtained from the the Internet Archive copy of the old E-Theses PDF (http://web.archive.org/web/20200220233832id_/http://othes.univie.ac.at/2419/1/2008-11-06_8700289.pdf, 10.4 MB, native text layer) and cross-checked against the u:theses Solr full_text field; the live Phaidra download (https://phaidra.univie.ac.at/download/o:12525…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yukuben is a three-tone language (high, mid, low) and has no stress accent (Druckakzent) at all; no position of prominence is given because none exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (The 'Akzent und Betonung' mention on p. 51-52 concerns Meinhof's Bantu vowel lengthening, not Yukuben.)
new_statements.identity_note: Weitzenauer 2008 does not name a dialect; her phonology section describes Yukuben in general (data drawn from Shimizu 1980 and Rennison's material). Prischnegg 2008 covers Yukuben together with Bete, Kapya, Kuteb, Lufu and Shibong (Akum) from 2004-2007 fieldwork per its abstract. Anyanwu 2013 (not open) distinguishes the Bā-lāābɘn and Bá-líssà dialects.
